2.  **Theoretical Background**:

This can be done in linear time $O(n+m)$ using a standard Breadth-First Search (BFS) or Depth-First Search (DFS). During the traversal, if we encounter an edge connecting two vertices of the same color (in a 2-coloring attempt), an odd cycle exists.

    *   In a 2-connected graph (or generally, if $u$ and $v$ are connected), the structure of cycles passing through them is rich. A known result in graph theory (often attributed to Robertson and Seymour or found in textbooks like Diestel) states that in a graph where $u$ and $v$ lie in the same biconnected component, there exist cycles through $u$ and $v$ of *different parity* (one odd, one even) if and only if there is an odd cycle through $u$ and $v$.
    *   More specifically, if there exists *any* odd cycle through $u$ and $v$, can we find it efficiently?

To restrict it to $u$ and $v$, we can perform a traversal (BFS/DFS) starting from $u$. We compute distances (mod 2) or simply a 2-coloring. If we find a back-edge creating an odd cycle, that cycle might not pass through $v$.
